feed.title: Combined summary - RFC: Two years of BIP Editing, time for some new faces?

entry.title: Combined summary - RFC: Two years of BIP Editing, time for some new faces?
entry.summary: Over the two-year period from April 2024 to April 2026, the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs) repository experienced a notably high level of activity and development. The BIP Editors facilitated extensive community engagement by managing over four thousand comments and handling nearly six hundred pull requests, with a substantial number of these being merged. Their stewardship led to the publication of forty-two new BIPs, signaling an ongoing evolution in both Bitcoin protocol standards and collaborative practices. Significant improvements were made to the repository’s processes and infrastructure, including updates to the continuous integration scripts and revisions to streamline the proposal workflow. These efforts have revitalized participation within the BIPs repository and contributed positively to broader Bitcoin development discussions. Despite these advancements, the operational burden of maintaining the repository was disproportionately carried by a minority of editors, particularly during periods when only one or two individuals managed most editorial duties. This highlighted the demanding nature of the role and prompted a consensus that a refreshed team of three dedicated editors would be optimal for sustaining effective governance of the repository. Such restructuring is intended to more evenly distribute responsibilities, foster consistent oversight, and ensure timely reviews of incoming proposals. Community input remains integral as proposed adjustments to the editorial structure are considered, reflecting the open-source ethos at the heart of Bitcoin development. The BIP Editor role requires a combination of technical expertise, diligence, and active community involvement. Editors must review and manage formal proposals, assess their clarity, technical soundness, and adherence to established guidelines. The position demands a solid foundation in Bitcoin’s technical landscape and strong organizational abilities for efficiently navigating the proposal pipeline. Candidates are expected to contribute at least five to ten hours per week, although actual commitment may often exceed this baseline. While certain editor-specific tasks like merging and labeling are reserved for those in the role, much of the review process benefits from broader community participation. Individuals interested in the position are encouraged to familiarize themselves with current open pull requests and contribute meaningful feedback through public channels, such as the [open pull requests section](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/pulls?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Apr+-label%3A%22Metadata+Update%22+-label%3ATypo-to-be-collected+-label%3ACI). Recent months have seen several community members express their willingness to join the BIP Editor team or intensify their contributions. Notably, Jaroslav Dlouhy reiterated his interest in becoming an editor, seeking guidance on the authorization process after having previously offered his assistance. Zed also expressed readiness to help, contingent upon how well the position aligns with his skill set. Daniela Brozzoni formally volunteered, providing details about her background as the author of BIP 394 and her experience with reviewing Bitcoin Core code. She committed to dedicating ten to fifteen hours weekly over the course of her master’s program in blockchain studies. Edil Medeiros similarly volunteered, emphasizing his professorial and peer-review credentials, as well as his leadership in research at Vinteum and active engagement in technical specification work, including output descriptors, Miniscript, and Stratum V2 as detailed in related [Vinteum blog posts](https://www.vinteum.org/blog/inside-a-vinteum-deep-dive-the-standards-behind-bitcoin-wallets) and [Stratum V2 write-up](https://www.vinteum.org/blog/inside-a-vinteum-deep-dive-bitcoin-mining-from-protocol-to-silicon). Both Daniela and Edil received substantial endorsements from other contributors, who praised their attention to detail, technical rigor, and commitment to community-driven standards. The discussion also addressed the ongoing challenges of managing the growing backlog of BIP submissions. Several high-quality proposals remain unreviewed for extended durations, partly due to limited editor availability. Contributions from non-editor reviewers such as Daniela and Edil have mitigated some of the workload, but the pace of incoming proposals continues to outstrip review capacity. Two main strategies were outlined for improving the situation: either expanding the team of active editors to better distribute the workload or reducing editorial standards to focus solely on format checks rather than comprehensive content evaluation. Maintaining rigorous review standards was deemed preferable, emphasizing the importance of quality assurance in proposal acceptance. To attract more volunteers without requiring long-term commitments, a term-limited approach—such as twelve to twenty-four month appointments—was suggested to encourage continuous renewal and sustained engagement. Community sentiment strongly favors refreshing the editorial team over lowering review standards. Multiple participants vouched for Daniela and Edil as suitable candidates, highlighting not only their technical capabilities but also their demonstrated reliability and collaborative spirit. Plebhash and Olaoluwa Osuntokun, among others, cited Daniela’s consistent review activity and Edil’s thoroughness and academic background as assets. Fanquake and Antoine Poinsot added further support, drawing on personal interactions and familiarity with the nominees’ contributions.
